headings.title: Introduction and Energy Balance Basics
headings.content: A **low calorie diet** generally restricts daily energy intake to about 1,000 to 1,500 calories for adults, creating a deliberate energy deficit. When the body burns more calories than it consumes, it is forced to tap into stored energy reserves, primarily adipose tissue, leading to weight loss. Understanding this basic principle of energy balance helps nurses explain weight management realistically to patients without relying on unproven fad diets.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Uses
headings.content:
Low calorie diets are frequently prescribed to manage clinical conditions where weight reduction significantly improves health outcomes. Common medical indications include:
- **Obesity**: Reducing body mass index to lower cardiovascular strain.
- **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus**: Improving glycemic control and insulin sensitivity.
- **Pre-operative Preparation**: Shrinking liver size prior to bariatric or major abdominal surgeries.
- **Obstructive Sleep Apnea**: Decreasing fat deposits around the neck to ease breathing during sleep.

headings.title: Nutritional Composition and Thresholds
headings.content:
Restricting calories does not mean abandoning good nutrition. A safe low calorie diet must still provide essential macronutrients and micronutrients to prevent malnutrition. 

- **Proteins**: Maintained at adequate levels to preserve lean muscle mass.
- **Carbohydrates**: Sourced primarily from complex, high-fiber foods to stabilize blood glucose.
- **Fats**: Included in small amounts of healthy unsaturated oils for cellular function and hormone production.
- **Vitamins and Minerals**: Often supplemented if total food volume is too low to meet daily micronutrient requirements.

headings.title: Patient Assessment and Screening
headings.content: Before initiating a calorie-restricted meal plan, nurses must perform a thorough baseline assessment. This includes calculating the body mass index, reviewing previous weight loss attempts, and screening for eating disorders or psychological barriers. Nurses also assess kidney and liver function labs to ensure the patient can safely handle metabolic shifts without organ strain.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Risks
headings.content: Rapid or unsupervised calorie restriction exposes patients to several physiological risks. Common complications include gallstone formation due to rapid mobilization of cholesterol, electrolyte imbalances, fatigue, and hair loss. Furthermore, severe restriction often triggers a compensatory drop in basal metabolic rate, making long-term weight maintenance much harder.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Education
headings.content: Nurses play a vital role in supporting patients through dietary changes. Interventions involve teaching portion control, encouraging regular physical activity, and helping patients set realistic weight loss goals of about 0.5 to 1 kilogram per week. Nurses should also advise patients to stay well-hydrated and report persistent dizziness, weakness, or mood changes.

headings.title: Monitoring Nutritional Status
headings.content: Continuous evaluation is necessary to ensure the diet is working safely. Nurses monitor changes in body weight, waist circumference, and vital signs during follow-up visits. Periodic blood tests track serum electrolytes, glucose, and lipid profiles to evaluate metabolic improvements and catch nutritional deficiencies early.
